<reason>Side B (PRO) won a close, well-fought debate by holding the cleaner comparative frame. Side A's strongest weapons — Singapore's low fertility despite public housing, Japan/Korea daycare expansion without births — were blunted by B's effective responses that these cases combined cash and affordability and thus indict both levers, leaving the marginal comparison to be decided by the Nordic/France-versus-Hungary/Japan contrast, which runs B's way. B also landed the sharpest turn of the debate: A's own example of families spending bonuses on "rent arrears" concedes that housing is the binding constraint, and a one-time payment covers one month of a decades-long cost structure. A's timing-rescue argument (pulling births from 35 to 31 prevents childlessness) was a genuinely clever analytical response, but B pressed it repeatedly and A never named a program that raised completed cohort fertility; A's like-for-like answer claiming lump sums "lifted second-birth shares" was the debate's most brittle unsupported specificity. A's "your lever needs three revolutions, mine needs an envelope" was memorable, but B's reply that cash is the weakest instrument facing the same headwinds, while childcare at least interacts with the motherhood penalty, held up. Both sides followed format honestly (clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure), used plausible background knowledge, and sharpened the clash over rounds; B simply resolved it more decisively on the metric that matters.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's rent-arrears turn: A named rent arrears as one use of flexible cash, and B converted it into a concession that housing is the binding constraint — "a one-time payment covers one month of arrears, while affordability fixes the decade" — which A never fully escaped and B crystallized in the closing as "recurring costs demand recurring relief."</best_rebuttal>
